defaults.permitted_development: Across Cambridgeshire, roof-lights are often permitted development where they stay low-profile, project no more than 150mm from the roof plane and do not rise above the existing roof height. The straightforward route can disappear if the property is listed, subject to local restrictions or if the proposal starts to read as a roof enlargement rather than a simple skylight.

rules.height_rules: Across Cambridgeshire, the roof-light should not make any part of the roof higher than it is now. A low-profile installation that leaves the original roof form dominant is generally the strongest option.
rules.depth_rules: Across Cambridgeshire, depth is controlled by projection from the roof plane rather than by the size of the opening alone. Once the unit projects more than 150mm, the straightforward householder route is usually lost.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Cambridgeshire, if the proposal creates a side-facing window, it should be obscure-glazed and any opening part should have its lowest edge at least 1.7 metres above the floor level of the room. Privacy and visible road-facing roof slopes deserve the earliest check.
rules.roof_rules: Across Cambridgeshire, a roof-light is easiest to defend when it remains subordinate to the slope and does not slide into dormer or terrace territory. Once the wider roof form changes materially, the normal roof-light route no longer tells the full story.
rules.materials_rules: Across Cambridgeshire, the best material strategy is usually visual restraint. Low-profile frames and clean flashings that work with the existing roof covering are less likely to jar with the roofscape than chunky or highly contrasting units.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status makes roof-lights more sensitive on visible elevations, particularly where a simple modern unit would cut across a traditional roof pattern.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required for roof-lights where the work alters historic roof fabric, framing, coverings or the character of the building.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the standard roof-light allowance survives everywhere: Article 4 controls and site-specific conditions can require an application for visible roof changes.

rules.permitted_development: In East Cambridgeshire, roof-lights are often permitted development where they stay low-profile, project no more than 150mm from the roof plane and do not rise above the existing roof height. rules.height_rules: A roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is controlled by projection from the roof plane rather than by the size of the opening alone. Once the unit projects more than 150mm, the straightforward householder route is usually lost.
rules.boundary_rules: The main boundary issue for roof-lights is overlooking. Where the opening is side-facing, obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum height to any opening part are the usual safeguards under the householder route.
rules.roof_rules: Think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Materials are not just about weathering: they control how visible the roof-light looks. Neat flashings, restrained frame colours and a low-profile unit usually sit better than bright trims or bulky cassettes.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Roof-specific planning conditions and Article 4 directions are a common reason why an otherwise modest roof-light still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: In Fenland, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: A roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: A roof-light is easiest to defend when it remains subordinate to the slope and does not slide into dormer or terrace territory. Once the wider roof form changes materially, the normal roof-light route no longer tells the full story.
rules.materials_rules: Use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.

rules.permitted_development: For houses in Huntingdonshire, the usual roof-light route is to keep the unit modest: no more than 150mm projection from the existing roof slope and no increase above the existing roof height. Once the proposal sits on a more sensitive roofscape or forms part of a larger roof alteration, planning permission is more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.

rules.height_rules: Height control for a roof-light is simple but strict: the proposal should not rise above the existing roof. The more flush and subordinate the unit appears, the easier the scheme is to keep within the normal householder route.
rules.depth_rules: Projection is one of the key measurable limits: no more than 150mm from the existing roof plane. If the proposal is too bulky, it can move out of the simple roof-light category and into a fuller planning assessment.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: Think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: Installing roof-lights in a listed building, or altering historic roof fabric within its curtilage, can require listed building consent even where the unit looks modest.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or roof-specific planning conditions can remove the usual householder right to add roof-lights, especially on visible elevations or in heritage areas.

rules.permitted_development: In Peterborough, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.
